hints: Focus on what atomisation really means, forming one mole of separate gaseous atoms starting from the element as it normally exists.
Check the starting state first, iodine is a solid at room conditions and sodium is also a solid, so any gas on the left is a warning sign.
Now check the amount made, you must finish with exactly one mole of gaseous atoms, so halve any equation that makes two moles.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of atomisation**

Think of it simply as pulling an element apart into single, lonely gas atoms. The definition is strict.

$$\text{element in standard state} \rightarrow 1\text{ mol of gaseous atoms}$$

**Check the standard state on the left**

Standard state means how the element naturally exists at 298 K and 1 atm. For sodium that is $\text{Na(s)}$, for iodine that is $\text{I}_2\text{(s)}$, for chlorine that is $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$.

So any equation starting with $\text{I}_2\text{(g)}$ is already wrong, even if the numbers look neat.

**Check for exactly one mole of atoms on the right**

Atomisation must make exactly $1$ mol of $\text{X(g)}$. That means $\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na(g)}$ is perfect, but $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl(g)}$ makes two moles and needs halving to $\frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Cl(g)}$.

**Rule out the different enthalpy change**

$\text{Na(g)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$ starts with an atom that is already gaseous and removes an electron. That is the first ionisation energy, not atomisation.

options.A: The stoichiometry is correct for one mole of atoms, but the reactant state is wrong. Standard iodine is $\text{I}_2\text{(s)}$, not $\text{I}_2\text{(g)}$. The correct atomisation would be $\frac{1}{2}\text{I}_2\text{(s)} \rightarrow \text{I(g)}$.
options.B: This fits the definition perfectly. Sodium's standard state is $\text{Na(s)}$ and the equation forms exactly one mole of gaseous atoms: $\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na(g)}$. This is the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of sodium.
options.C: The states are correct because chlorine is $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$, but it forms two moles of atoms instead of one. Atomisation must give $1$ mol of $\text{Cl(g)}$, so the equation should be $\frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Cl(g)}$. This is a common trap with diatomic elements.
options.D: This starts from an already gaseous atom and forms an ion and an electron. That is the definition of the first ionisation energy of sodium, not atomisation. Atomisation must start from the element in its standard state, $\text{Na(s)}$.
